headings.title: Introduction and Overview of Male Sexually Transmitted Infections
headings.content: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) represent a major public health concern globally and hold significant relevance in nursing practice within Nigeria. In male patients, STIs encompass a diverse group of bacterial, viral, fungal, and parasitic infections primarily acquired through sexual contact, including vaginal, anal, and oral intercourse. For nursing students preparing for professional examinations, understanding male STIs is critical because early identification and intervention prevent severe long-term complications such as infertility, chronic pain, and systemic disease. Furthermore, nurses often serve as the primary point of contact in community health clinics and hospitals, making them vital educators in promoting safe sex practices and reducing the stigma associated with seeking care. In many resource-constrained settings across Nigeria, men may delay seeking treatment due to cultural stigmas or fear of judgment. Therefore, cultivating a non-judgmental, culturally competent approach is essential for effective nursing assessment and patient rapport. By mastering the fundamentals of male STIs, nursing students will be better equipped to provide comprehensive holistic care, implement effective health promotion campaigns, and contribute to the reduction of disease transmission rates within vulnerable populations.

headings.title: Common Pathogens and Classifications
headings.content: Sexually transmitted infections in men are caused by a wide variety of microorganisms, which are typically classified based on their causative agents into bacterial, viral, protozoal, and fungal pathogens. Bacterial STIs, such as Neisseria gonorrhoeae (the causative agent of gonorrhea) and Chlamydia trachomatis, are among the most frequently reported bacterial infections and are known for causing urethritis and purulent discharge. Another significant bacterial pathogen is Treponema pallidum, the spirochete responsible for syphilis, which progresses through distinct clinical stages if left untreated. Viral pathogens include human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) which causes painful genital lesions, and human papillomavirus (HPV), which can lead to genital warts and malignancies. Parasitic and protozoal infections, though less common in pure male presentation compared to vaginal trichomoniasis, can still affect the male urogenital tract, with Trichomonas vaginalis occasionally colonizing the urethra or prostate. Fungal infections, such as candidiasis, may also occur, particularly in uncircumcised males or immunocompromised patients. Categorizing these pathogens accurately helps nursing students understand the distinct pathophysiological mechanisms, transmission dynamics, and specific pharmacological treatments required for each specific class of infection.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Modes of Transmission
headings.content: The pathophysiology of male STIs involves the direct invasion of mucosal surfaces of the urogenital tract, rectum, or oropharynx by infectious pathogens. Once pathogens breach the epithelial barrier, they often trigger localized inflammatory responses, leading to tissue damage, cellular destruction, and recruitment of immune cells such as neutrophils and lymphocytes. For instance, Neisseria gonorrhoeae utilizes pili and outer membrane proteins to attach to columnar epithelial cells of the urethra, provoking a robust neutrophilic response that results in the characteristic purulent urethral discharge. Modes of transmission are predominantly sexual, occurring via unprotected vaginal, anal, or oral intercourse where mucosal-to-mucosal contact facilitates pathogen transfer. Additionally, vertical transmission from an infected mother to a neonate can occur during childbirth, and blood-borne transmission is common for viral agents like HIV and Hepatitis B through sharing needles or contaminated blood products. Understanding these pathways is crucial for nursing students, as it highlights the exact biological mechanisms that allow infections to take hold and spread within populations. Knowledge of transmission routes also directly informs the planning of targeted educational interventions aimed at interrupting the transmission chain.

headings.title: Clinical Manifestations and Signs in Male Patients
headings.content: Clinical manifestations of STIs in men vary widely depending on the specific pathogen involved, and a significant proportion of infections can remain entirely asymptomatic, serving as hidden reservoirs for community transmission. When symptoms do appear, common signs include urethral discharge (which may be clear, mucopurulent, or thick yellow-green), dysuria (pain or burning sensation during urination), and pruritus or irritation within the urethral meatus. Patients may also present with scrotal pain, swelling, or tenderness, indicative of complications such as epididymitis or orchitis. Dermatological findings are also frequent; painless or painful genital ulcers, vesicles, or papules can indicate conditions like primary syphilis, chancroid, or genital herpes. Inguinal lymphadenopathy (swollen, tender lymph nodes in the groin) is another common physical sign associated with ulcerative STIs. Furthermore, rectal pain, discharge, or bleeding may occur in men who engage in receptive anal intercourse. For nursing students, performing a thorough physical assessment and taking a detailed, sensitive sexual history are vital skills for recognizing these diverse clinical signs and ensuring prompt referral for diagnostic confirmation.

headings.title: Diagnostic Evaluation and Screening Tests
headings.content: Accurate diagnostic evaluation and screening are essential components of managing male STIs, enabling healthcare providers to confirm infections and initiate appropriate targeted therapies. Diagnostic modalities depend heavily on the suspected pathogen and the anatomical site of exposure. Nucleic Acid Amplification Tests (NAATs) are currently considered the gold standard for detecting bacterial pathogens such as Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae, utilizing first-catch urine samples or urethral swabs due to their exceptionally high sensitivity and specificity. Gram staining of urethral smears remains a rapid, useful diagnostic tool in resource-limited clinical settings for identifying gram-negative intracellular diplococci indicative of gonorrhea. Serological blood tests are indispensable for diagnosing systemic viral and bacterial infections; for instance, treponemal and non-treponemal tests (such as VDRL or RPR) are used to diagnose syphilis, while enzyme immunoassay and rapid diagnostic tests are standard for HIV screening. Additionally, viral culture or PCR swab tests are utilized when active vesicular lesions characteristic of herpes simplex virus are present. Nursing students must understand specimen collection protocols, patient preparation instructions (such as avoiding urination for a specific time prior to NAAT urine collection), and the importance of confidentiality during the diagnostic process.

headings.title: Pharmacological Management and Nursing Interventions
headings.content: Pharmacological management of male STIs requires precise adherence to evidence-based treatment guidelines, combining curative therapies with comprehensive nursing interventions. Bacterial infections are typically managed with specific antibiotic regimens; for example, uncomplicated gonorrhea is often treated with dual therapy such as intramuscular ceftriaxone and oral azithromycin to prevent antimicrobial resistance, while chlamydia is treated with azithromycin or doxycycline. Viral infections, such as HSV and HIV, cannot be cured completely, but antiviral medications (like acyclovir, valacyclovir, or antiretroviral therapy) successfully suppress viral replication, reduce symptom duration, and decrease transmission risks. Nursing interventions extend far beyond administering medications; nurses are responsible for educating patients on the absolute necessity of completing full antibiotic courses even if symptoms resolve. Nurses must also coordinate partner notification and treatment to prevent immediate reinfection, a critical step in breaking the transmission cycle. Furthermore, nurses provide supportive care for symptoms such as pain, counsel patients on abstaining from sexual activity during the treatment window, and ensure proper follow-up scheduling to confirm treatment efficacy.

headings.title: Potential Complications of Untreated STIs in Men
headings.content: Untreated or inadequately managed sexually transmitted infections in men can lead to severe, debilitating, and sometimes irreversible long-term complications affecting the urogenital, reproductive, and systemic organ systems. Localized complications of ascending bacterial infections such as chlamydia and gonorrhea include epididymitis, prostatitis, and orchitis, which can cause chronic pelvic or scrotal pain and, in severe cases, result in male factor infertility due to obstruction or damage of the reproductive ducts. Urethral strictures—scarring and narrowing of the urethral lumen—can also develop following chronic or recurrent urethritis, leading to severe obstructive voiding symptoms and urinary tract infections. Systemic complications are particularly prominent in untreated syphilis, which can progress from primary and secondary stages to latent and tertiary syphilis, causing devastating cardiovascular damage (such as aortitis) and neurosyphilis. Furthermore, the presence of untreated inflammatory STIs, particularly those causing genital ulcerations, significantly increases the biological susceptibility to acquiring and transmitting human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). For nursing students, recognizing these profound risks underscores why prompt diagnosis, rigorous patient adherence, and public health follow-up are absolute priorities in clinical practice.

headings.title: Patient Education, Prevention, and Public Health Strategies
headings.content: Patient education, primary prevention, and public health strategies form the cornerstone of controlling the spread of sexually transmitted infections among men. Primary prevention strategies focus on promoting consistent and correct condom use, encouraging reductions in high-risk sexual behaviors, and expanding access to vaccination programs, such as HPV and Hepatitis B vaccines. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) also play expanding roles in public health frameworks to prevent HIV acquisition among high-risk individuals. Patient education delivered by nurses must be clear, culturally sensitive, and tailored to the target audience, addressing common misconceptions about STI transmission and symptom presentation. Public health strategies involve robust partner tracing, confidential screening programs in community and occupational settings, and the implementation of syndromic management protocols where laboratory testing is immediately unavailable. In Nigeria and similar regions, community-based health outreaches led by nursing professionals are vital for reaching men who may not otherwise access formal healthcare facilities. By empowering patients with knowledge on safe sex, early symptom recognition, and the importance of completing treatments, nurses actively contribute to reducing overall disease incidence and fostering healthier communities.
